clinicalPearls: A common and distressing complication after anaesthesia that reduces patient satisfaction, delays discharge, and occasionally causes serious complications
Established patient risk factors include female sex, non-smoking status, history of PONV or motion sickness, and younger age, often summarised in simplified risk scores
Anaesthetic and surgical factors include use of volatile agents and nitrous oxide, perioperative opioids, and longer or certain types of surgery
A multimodal approach works best: reducing baseline risk (opioid-sparing analgesia, regional techniques, total intravenous anaesthesia) and combining antiemetics from different classes
Prophylactic agents span several receptor targets, including serotonin antagonists, corticosteroids, dopamine antagonists, and antihistamines, chosen according to risk
For breakthrough symptoms, an antiemetic from a class not already used for prophylaxis is preferred rather than repeating the same drug
Adequate hydration, avoidance of unnecessary opioids, and treatment of pain and hypotension help reduce symptoms
Persistent or severe postoperative vomiting should prompt consideration of surgical, metabolic, or intracranial causes rather than assuming simple PONV
reference.pathophysiology: Nausea and vomiting are coordinated by brainstem centres receiving input from the chemoreceptor trigger zone, vestibular system, higher cortical centres, and vagal afferents from the gastrointestinal tract. Multiple neurotransmitters, including serotonin, dopamine, histamine, acetylcholine, and substance P, mediate these pathways. Anaesthetic agents, opioids, gastric distension, hypotension, and surgical stimulation activate one or more of these inputs. Because several receptor systems contribute, blocking a single pathway is often insufficient, which is why combining antiemetics acting at different receptors is more effective than escalating a single agent.
additionalDifferentials: Raised intracranial pressure or neurological cause
Metabolic disturbance such as hyponatraemia or hypoglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of hydration, pain, and haemodynamics
Review of anaesthetic and analgesic agents administered
Electrolytes and glucose if vomiting is persistent
Abdominal imaging if obstruction or ileus is suspected
Neurological assessment if a central cause is possible
redFlags: Persistent vomiting causing dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, or aspiration risk
Vomiting with headache, focal neurology, or reduced consciousness suggesting an intracranial cause
Bilious or feculent vomiting indicating bowel obstruction
Vomiting with severe abdominal pain suggesting a surgical complication
reference.prognosis: PONV is usually self-limiting and responds to multimodal prophylaxis and treatment, but uncontrolled symptoms can delay recovery, cause dehydration, and rarely lead to aspiration or wound complications.
pitfalls: Relying on a single antiemetic in high-risk patients instead of combining agents
Repeating the same drug class for breakthrough symptoms
Overlooking modifiable contributors such as opioids, hypotension, and dehydration
Assuming all postoperative vomiting is benign and missing a surgical or neurological cause
Failing to risk-stratify and tailor prophylaxis preoperatively
management: Reduction of baseline risk with opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia, regional anaesthetic techniques and total intravenous anaesthesia using propofol while avoiding volatile agents and nitrous oxide

Multimodal antiemetic prophylaxis combining agents from different receptor classes, such as serotonin-receptor antagonists, the corticosteroid dexamethasone, dopamine antagonists, antihistamines, an anticholinergic patch and a neurokinin-receptor antagonist, according to risk
Treatment of breakthrough symptoms with an antiemetic from a class not already used for prophylaxis rather than repeating the same drug
Supportive care with intravenous fluids for hydration and correction of electrolyte disturbance from persistent vomiting
Correction of contributing factors including uncontrolled pain, hypotension and gastric distension
Escalation and investigation for a surgical or central cause when vomiting is persistent, with imaging if obstruction or ileus is suspected
